title: Veracity and Fidelity

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Each principle answers a different question about the same action. Nonmaleficence asks 'does this hurt the patient?' Autonomy asks 'whose decision is this?' Fidelity asks 'did I keep faith with what I committed to?' Veracity asks a narrower question than any of them: 'does what I just said match reality?' When you are trying to name a principle, find the question it asks — that is faster and more reliable than matching vocabulary.

### Question 2

Fidelity is what makes a professional relationship something a patient can rely on rather than a series of separate transactions. Notice that a professional relationship carries two kinds of commitment: explicit ones you state out loud ('I'll be back at three'), and implied ones you never say because entering the role creates them (that you will monitor them, advocate for them, and not abandon them mid-shift). Fidelity covers both, which is why it is broader than simply keeping your word.

### Question 3

The useful test is not 'was every sentence true?' but 'what belief am I trying to produce, and is that belief accurate?' Someone who reports the one reassuring lab value and skips the three concerning ones has said nothing false and still aimed the listener at a false conclusion. Deception is defined by the intended effect on the other person's understanding, which is why it can be accomplished entirely with true statements.

### Question 4

Watch what option D quietly does: it treats truth as a technique for producing agreement. If that were the purpose, then truth would become optional the moment a lie worked better, and the principle would collapse into persuasion. Veracity is valuable precisely because it holds when it is inconvenient — a patient who learns the truth and then refuses the recommended treatment is evidence the principle worked, not that it failed.

### Question 5

The real cost is not the individual lie but the loss of a signal. Reassurance only reduces anxiety because it is understood to be conditional on the facts; if it is given unconditionally, it carries zero information and stops reassuring anyone. This is why the harm compounds across a unit — the clinician who is being honest today inherits the credibility that everyone else has already spent.

### Question 6

The clearest way to keep them apart is to find cases where only one fails. A nurse who honestly reports 'I said I would return and I never did' has satisfied veracity while breaching fidelity. A nurse who reliably appears every hour but shades what she tells the patient has satisfied fidelity while breaching veracity. Two independent tests means two independent ways to fail, which is why naming the right one matters when analyzing a case.

### Question 7

The doctrine shifted for an evidentiary reason: clinicians turned out to be poor predictors of who could not handle bad news, and their predictions tracked their own discomfort more closely than the patient's actual resilience. So the question changed from 'can this person handle it?' to 'whose information is it?' That reframing also explains why a patient declining details is fine while a family declining on her behalf is not — one is the owner of the information choosing, the other is someone else choosing for her.

### Question 8

Promises are usually broken by workflow, not by intent — the nurse who said 'twenty minutes' gets pulled into a rapid response and the commitment dies with the shift. That diagnosis points to the fix: commitments need a place to live outside one person's memory, and they need an update path when circumstances change. It also explains why eliminating promises is the wrong solution. The patient waiting in pain needs a time estimate; withdrawing the estimate transfers the burden of uncertainty onto them so the unit never has to be accountable for it.

### Question 9

There is a clean diagnostic for deception: ask whether the intervention would still work if you narrated it accurately. Telling a patient exactly what is in a syringe of morphine changes nothing about how it works. Telling her the syringe holds saline destroys the entire plan. Anything whose effectiveness depends on the other person remaining misinformed is deceptive by construction — and note that this is what separates a concealed placebo from an open-label placebo, which is disclosed and therefore does not offend veracity.

### Question 10

Two ideas get conflated here. 'No harm resulted' is a statement about outcome; 'nothing happened' is a statement about fact. Something did happen, to this person's body, and the information belongs to her first — her judgment about whether it matters is hers to make, not the nurse's to make on her behalf. The second half of disclosure is equally important: an honest account includes what is being done about it, because 'this occurred' without 'and here is our response' leaves the patient holding a problem alone.

### Question 11

Honesty constrains content, not pace. Nothing in veracity says all true information must arrive at once, and 'what have you been told so far?' is not stalling — it is finding out which false beliefs, if any, are already in place, since correcting those is the honest work. Look at what the three wrong answers share: each ends the conversation. A and B change the subject, C hands it off with a fabricated excuse. Whatever else truthfulness requires, it rules out leaving the person alone with the question they just asked.

### Question 12

The decisive move is recognizing that some promises are wrong to make, not merely hard to keep. Once the nurse says yes, she has manufactured a genuine conflict between two duties she now holds — and the family, not the patient, will have authored it. Declining is also not a rejection of the family: their fear is usually real and worth exploring, and the productive response is to bring them into how the news is delivered rather than into whether it is. What cannot happen is pledging the same loyalty in two opposite directions.
